description: Dilated Cardiomyopathy (DCM) is a heart disease characterized by the enlargement and weakening of the heart's chambers, leading to decreased heart function and eventual heart failure.
common_species: Dog (most common in large breeds, but can occur in cats)
symptoms: Coughing (particularly at night or after exercise)
Weight loss or poor weight gain
Abdominal distension (due to fluid buildup, ascites)

symptoms.symptom: Coughing (particularly at night or after exercise)
Weight loss or poor weight gain
Fluid accumulation in the lungs (pulmonary edema)

physical_examination: Auscultation of heart for abnormal sounds (e.g., heart murmurs)
Palpation of abdomen for fluid buildup (ascites)
Observation of clinical signs (exercise intolerance, coughing, etc.)
diagnostic_tests: Echocardiogram (to visualize heart size and function)
Electrocardiogram (ECG) to detect arrhythmias
Chest X-rays to assess heart size and fluid buildup
Blood pressure measurement
Blood tests to check for biomarkers (e.g., cardiac troponin)

medications.purpose: To reduce blood pressure and heart strain

medications.dosage_dog: 2–4 mg/kg orally or intravenously every 8–12 hours
medications.dosage_cat: 1–2 mg/kg orally or intravenously every 12 hours

dietary_management.purpose: To address potential deficiencies linked to DCM

other_treatments.purpose: For severe respiratory distress
To reduce strain on the heart

references: Textbook of Veterinary Internal Medicine by Stephen J. Ettinger & Edward C. Feldman
Veterinary Clinics of North America: Small Animal Practice
Current Veterinary Therapy

description: Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy (HCM) is a condition where the heart muscle (myocardium) thickens, reducing the heart's ability to pump blood effectively. It is most commonly seen in cats and can lead to heart failure, arrhythmias, and sudden death.
common_species: Cat (most common in cats, rare in dogs)
differential_diagnoses: Asthma (in cats, due to similar breathing difficulties)
Hyperthyroidism (as it can lead to similar heart conditions)

physical_examination: Auscultation of heart for abnormal sounds (e.g., heart murmurs or gallop rhythm)
Observation of clinical signs such as labored breathing, lethargy
diagnostic_tests: Echocardiogram (to visualize the thickening of the heart muscle)
Electrocardiogram (ECG) to detect arrhythmias
Chest X-rays to assess heart size and fluid buildup
Blood pressure measurement
Blood tests (including thyroid levels, especially in older cats)

medications.purpose: To slow the heart rate and reduce oxygen demand
To relax the heart muscle and improve heart function

medications.dosage_dog: 1–2 mg/kg orally or intravenously every 8–12 hours
medications.dosage_cat: 1 mg/kg orally or intravenously every 12 hours
medications.purpose: To remove excess fluid if congestive heart failure is present
To reduce blood pressure and the heart's workload
To reduce the risk of blood clots forming

dietary_management.purpose: To prevent fluid retention and reduce heart strain

other_treatments.purpose: For severe respiratory distress
To reduce strain on the heart

references: Textbook of Veterinary Internal Medicine by Stephen J. Ettinger & Edward C. Feldman
Veterinary Clinics of North America: Small Animal Practice
Current Veterinary Therapy

description: Restrictive Cardiomyopathy (RCM) is a form of heart disease where the walls of the ventricles become stiff but not thickened, leading to poor ventricular filling and reduced heart function. It is most commonly seen in cats and is associated with heart failure and arrhythmias.
common_species: Cat (more common), rare in dogs
differential_diagnoses: Feline Asthma (due to similar respiratory signs)

physical_examination: Auscultation of heart for abnormal sounds (e.g., heart murmurs)
Observation of labored breathing and fluid accumulation in the abdomen or chest
diagnostic_tests: Echocardiogram (to evaluate heart function and wall stiffness)
Chest X-rays to check for fluid buildup (pleural effusion or ascites)
Electrocardiogram (ECG) to detect arrhythmias
Blood tests to assess overall organ function and check for heart-related biomarkers

medications.dosage_dog: 2–4 mg/kg orally or intravenously every 8–12 hours
medications.dosage_cat: 1–2 mg/kg orally or intravenously every 12 hours

medications.purpose: To reduce blood pressure and heart strain
To relax the heart muscle and improve heart function
To reduce heart rate and improve heart function

dietary_management.purpose: To reduce fluid retention and heart strain

other_treatments.purpose: For severe respiratory distress
To remove accumulated fluid from the chest or abdomen

references: Textbook of Veterinary Internal Medicine by Stephen J. Ettinger & Edward C. Feldman
Veterinary Clinics of North America: Small Animal Practice
Current Veterinary Therapy

description: Arrhythmogenic Right Ventricular Cardiomyopathy (ARVC) is a hereditary heart disease that primarily affects the right ventricle, where the muscle tissue is replaced by fatty or fibrous tissue. This results in abnormal heart rhythms (arrhythmias), leading to fainting, weakness, and in some cases, sudden death. It is most commonly seen in certain dog breeds.
common_species: Dog (especially Boxers, also seen in English Bulldogs)

physical_examination: Auscultation of heart for abnormal sounds (e.g., heart murmurs, arrhythmias)
Observation of clinical signs such as fainting or collapse
diagnostic_tests: Electrocardiogram (ECG) to detect arrhythmias
Holter monitoring (24-hour ECG) to evaluate intermittent arrhythmias
Echocardiogram to evaluate the structure of the right ventricle
Genetic testing (especially for Boxers) to identify ARVC mutation
Chest X-rays to evaluate heart size and rule out other causes

medications.purpose: To reduce the heart rate and improve heart function

dietary_management.purpose: To reduce fluid retention and heart strain

other_treatments.purpose: To prevent arrhythmias and fainting episodes
For severe cases with life-threatening arrhythmias

references: Textbook of Veterinary Internal Medicine by Stephen J. Ettinger & Edward C. Feldman
Veterinary Clinics of North America: Small Animal Practice
Current Veterinary Therapy
Cardiology of the Dog and Cat by Dr. Lawrence Tilley & Naomi Burtnick

description: Mitral Valve Disease (MVD) is a degenerative condition of the mitral valve, located between the left atrium and left ventricle of the heart. Over time, the valve becomes thickened and distorted, leading to improper closure, regurgitation of blood, and eventual heart failure. It is especially common in small breed dogs.
common_species: Dog (especially small breeds such as Cavalier King Charles Spaniels)
main_symptom: Coughing, particularly at night or after exercise
symptoms: Coughing (especially at night or after exercise)

physical_examination: Auscultation of heart for a characteristic mitral valve murmur
Observation of clinical signs such as coughing and labored breathing
diagnostic_tests: Echocardiogram (to visualize mitral valve degeneration and regurgitation)
Chest X-rays to assess heart size and presence of fluid in the lungs
Electrocardiogram (ECG) to detect arrhythmias
Blood pressure measurement (as MVD can lead to hypertension)

medications.purpose: To reduce blood pressure and heart strain

medications.dosage_dog: 2–4 mg/kg orally or intravenously every 8–12 hours
medications.purpose: To remove excess fluid from the lungs
To reduce the heart rate and improve heart function

dietary_management.purpose: To reduce fluid retention and heart strain

other_treatments.purpose: For severe respiratory distress
To prevent worsening of symptoms

references: Textbook of Veterinary Internal Medicine by Stephen J. Ettinger & Edward C. Feldman
Veterinary Clinics of North America: Small Animal Practice
Current Veterinary Therapy
Cardiology of the Dog and Cat by Dr. Lawrence Tilley & Naomi Burtnick

description: Tricuspid Valve Dysplasia (TVD) is a congenital heart defect characterized by malformation of the tricuspid valve, which is located between the right atrium and right ventricle. This leads to improper valve closure, blood regurgitation, and right-sided heart failure. TVD is most commonly seen in certain dog breeds.
common_species: Dog (particularly Labrador Retrievers and Golden Retrievers)
main_symptom: Abdominal distension (ascites) due to fluid buildup

physical_examination: Auscultation of heart for murmurs on the right side (indicative of tricuspid valve malfunction)
Observation of abdominal distension and jugular vein distension
diagnostic_tests: Echocardiogram (to assess tricuspid valve malformation and blood regurgitation)
Chest X-rays to evaluate heart size and fluid accumulation in the abdomen or chest
Electrocardiogram (ECG) to detect arrhythmias
Blood pressure measurement to evaluate systemic effects

medications.dosage_dog: 2–4 mg/kg orally or intravenously every 8–12 hours
medications.purpose: To reduce fluid buildup (ascites and pleural effusion)
To reduce blood pressure and heart strain
To reduce the heart rate and improve heart function

dietary_management.purpose: To reduce fluid retention and heart strain

other_treatments.purpose: To remove excess fluid from the abdomen in cases of severe ascites
For severe respiratory distress
To reduce heart strain and prevent worsening of symptoms

description: Myxomatous Mitral Valve Disease (MMVD) is a chronic degenerative condition of the mitral valve, characterized by thickening and deformity of the valve's structure, leading to valve leakage (regurgitation) and eventual heart failure. It is especially common in small breed dogs and is the most common acquired heart disease in dogs.
common_species: Dog (especially small breeds like Cavalier King Charles Spaniels, Miniature Poodles, and Dachshunds)
main_symptom: Coughing, especially at night or after exercise
symptoms: Coughing (particularly at night or after exercise)

symptoms.symptom: Coughing (especially after exercise or at night)

physical_examination: Auscultation of heart for characteristic mitral valve murmur
Observation of clinical signs like coughing and labored breathing
diagnostic_tests: Echocardiogram (to visualize mitral valve degeneration and regurgitation)
Chest X-rays to assess heart size and presence of fluid in the lungs
Electrocardiogram (ECG) to detect arrhythmias
Blood pressure measurement (as MMVD can lead to hypertension)

medications.purpose: To reduce blood pressure and heart strain

medications.dosage_dog: 2–4 mg/kg orally or intravenously every 8–12 hours
medications.purpose: To reduce fluid buildup in the lungs
To reduce heart rate and improve heart function

dietary_management.purpose: To reduce fluid retention and heart strain

To prevent worsening of symptoms

description: Endocardiosis, also known as Myxomatous Mitral Valve Disease (MMVD), is a degenerative condition affecting the heart valves, most commonly the mitral valve. It leads to thickening and deformation of the valve, resulting in improper closure, regurgitation of blood, and eventual heart failure. It is particularly common in small breed dogs.
common_species: Dog (especially small breeds like Cavalier King Charles Spaniels, Miniature Poodles, and Dachshunds)
main_symptom: Coughing, especially at night or after exercise
symptoms: Coughing (particularly at night or after exercise)

symptoms.symptom: Coughing (especially after exercise or at night)

Observation of clinical signs like coughing and labored breathing
diagnostic_tests: Echocardiogram (to visualize mitral valve degeneration and regurgitation)
Chest X-rays to assess heart size and presence of fluid in the lungs
Electrocardiogram (ECG) to detect arrhythmias
Blood pressure measurement (as Endocardiosis can lead to hypertension)

medications.purpose: To reduce blood pressure and heart strain

description: Pulmonic Stenosis is a congenital heart defect characterized by a narrowing of the pulmonary valve, obstructing blood flow from the right ventricle to the lungs. It leads to right-sided heart enlargement and failure over time.
common_species: Dog (especially small breeds like English Bulldogs, Beagles, and Boxers)

physical_examination: Auscultation of heart for a murmur on the left side
Jugular vein distension in severe cases
diagnostic_tests: Echocardiogram (to assess the degree of stenosis and heart enlargement)
Chest X-rays (to assess heart size)
Electrocardiogram (ECG) for arrhythmias

medications.purpose: To reduce heart rate and improve heart function

other_treatments.purpose: Surgical correction for severe stenosis

description: Aortic Stenosis is a congenital heart condition characterized by narrowing of the aortic valve, obstructing blood flow from the left ventricle to the aorta. This results in left-sided heart enlargement and possible heart failure.
common_species: Dog (especially large breeds like Boxers, Golden Retrievers, and German Shepherds)

physical_examination: Auscultation of heart for a murmur on the left side
Palpation for pulse deficits
diagnostic_tests: Echocardiogram (to assess the severity of the stenosis)
Chest X-rays (to check heart size and structure)
ECG for arrhythmias

medications.purpose: To reduce heart rate and improve heart function

other_treatments.purpose: Less effective for aortic stenosis, but may be used in severe cases

description: Patent Ductus Arteriosus (PDA) is a congenital heart defect in which the ductus arteriosus, a blood vessel that bypasses the lungs in the fetus, fails to close after birth. This causes abnormal blood flow between the aorta and the pulmonary artery.
common_species: Dog (especially small breeds like Toy Poodles and Shetland Sheepdogs, often in female puppies)

physical_examination: Auscultation of heart for a continuous murmur
Observation of clinical signs like coughing and exercise intolerance
diagnostic_tests: Echocardiogram (to visualize abnormal blood flow between the aorta and pulmonary artery)
Chest X-rays (to assess heart size and lung condition)
ECG for arrhythmias

medications.purpose: To reduce fluid buildup in lungs

other_treatments.purpose: Correction of PDA via surgical closure
Minimally invasive closure for PDA

description: Ventricular Septal Defect (VSD) is a congenital heart defect characterized by an abnormal opening in the septum between the heart's two ventricles, leading to abnormal blood flow between the chambers.
common_species: Dog, Cat

physical_examination: Auscultation of heart for a murmur
Observation of clinical signs like coughing and weakness
diagnostic_tests: Echocardiogram (to visualize abnormal blood flow through the septal defect)
Chest X-rays (to assess heart size)
ECG for arrhythmias

medications.purpose: To reduce fluid buildup in lungs

other_treatments.purpose: Closure of the septal defect through surgery, recommended for large defects

description: Atrial Septal Defect (ASD) is a congenital heart condition characterized by an abnormal opening in the septum between the heart's two atria, leading to abnormal blood flow between the chambers.
common_species: Dog, Cat

physical_examination: Auscultation of heart for a murmur
Observation of clinical signs like coughing and weakness
diagnostic_tests: Echocardiogram (to visualize abnormal blood flow through the septal defect)
Chest X-rays (to assess heart size)
ECG for arrhythmias

medications.purpose: To reduce fluid buildup in lungs

other_treatments.purpose: Closure of the septal defect through surgery, often necessary for large defects

description: Tetralogy of Fallot is a congenital heart defect composed of four abnormalities: pulmonary stenosis, ventricular septal defect, right ventricular hypertrophy, and an overriding aorta. It results in poor oxygenation of blood and can cause cyanosis.
common_species: Dog (especially small breeds like Keeshonds, Miniature Poodles)

physical_examination: Observation of cyanosis
Auscultation for murmurs
diagnostic_tests: Echocardiogram (to assess the structural abnormalities)
Chest X-rays (to assess heart and lung function)
ECG for arrhythmias

medications.purpose: To reduce heart rate and improve oxygenation

other_treatments.purpose: Surgery to address structural defects

description: Cor Triatriatum is a rare congenital heart defect in which an abnormal membrane divides one of the atria into two chambers, leading to abnormal blood flow through the heart and increased pressure in the atria.
common_species: Dog, Cat (rare)

physical_examination: Auscultation for abnormal heart sounds
Observation of labored breathing
diagnostic_tests: Echocardiogram (to visualize the abnormal membrane in the atria)
Chest X-rays (to assess heart size and lung condition)
ECG for arrhythmias

other_treatments.purpose: Surgical removal of the membrane

description: Ebstein's Anomaly is a congenital heart defect in which the tricuspid valve is displaced towards the apex of the right ventricle, leading to right-sided heart enlargement and heart failure.
common_species: Dog (rare)

physical_examination: Auscultation for tricuspid regurgitation
Observation of jugular vein distension
diagnostic_tests: Echocardiogram (to assess tricuspid valve displacement)
Chest X-rays (to evaluate heart size)
ECG for arrhythmias

other_treatments.purpose: Surgical repair of the tricuspid valve

description: Vascular Ring Anomalies are congenital malformations of the major blood vessels that can encircle the esophagus or trachea, leading to compression and obstruction of the esophagus, causing regurgitation and difficulty swallowing.
common_species: Dog (especially large breeds like German Shepherds)

physical_examination: Palpation for esophageal dilation
Observation of regurgitation
diagnostic_tests: Barium swallow radiography (to visualize the esophagus and detect obstruction)
Chest X-rays (to assess esophageal dilation)
Echocardiogram (to evaluate blood vessel anatomy)

other_treatments.purpose: Surgical removal of the constricting vessel

description: Atrial Fibrillation (AF) is an abnormal heart rhythm characterized by rapid, uncoordinated contractions of the atria. This leads to inefficient blood flow and can cause heart failure over time. It is commonly associated with underlying heart disease.
common_species: Dog (especially large breeds like Dobermans, Great Danes)

physical_examination: Auscultation for irregular heart sounds
Observation of pulse deficits
diagnostic_tests: Electrocardiogram (ECG) to detect the irregular rhythm
Echocardiogram to evaluate heart size and function
Holter monitor (24-hour ECG) to detect intermittent arrhythmias

other_treatments.purpose: Used to restore normal heart rhythm in severe cases

description: Ventricular Arrhythmias are abnormal heart rhythms originating from the ventricles, which can lead to life-threatening complications such as ventricular tachycardia or fibrillation. It often occurs due to underlying heart disease or myocardial injury.
common_species: Dog (especially Dobermans and Boxers, breeds prone to heart disease)

physical_examination: Auscultation for abnormal heart sounds
Observation of clinical signs like fainting
diagnostic_tests: Electrocardiogram (ECG) to detect ventricular arrhythmias
Echocardiogram to assess heart size and structure
Holter monitor (24-hour ECG) for intermittent arrhythmias

other_treatments.purpose: Used in emergency cases to restore normal rhythm

description: Sick Sinus Syndrome (SSS) is a condition characterized by abnormal function of the sinoatrial node (the heart's natural pacemaker), leading to periods of abnormally slow heart rates (bradycardia), pauses, or even fainting.
common_species: Dog (especially Miniature Schnauzers, Cocker Spaniels, and West Highland Terriers)

physical_examination: Auscultation for bradycardia
Observation of syncope or collapse
diagnostic_tests: Electrocardiogram (ECG) to detect sinus pauses and bradycardia
Holter monitor (24-hour ECG) to detect intermittent bradycardia
Echocardiogram to rule out structural heart disease

medications.purpose: To increase heart rate during episodes

other_treatments.purpose: Permanent solution for controlling heart rate

description: Atrial Standstill is a condition in which the atria stop contracting, often associated with severe hyperkalemia or underlying muscular dystrophy. This results in bradycardia and can lead to heart failure or sudden collapse.
common_species: Dog (especially English Springer Spaniels)

physical_examination: Auscultation for a slow heart rate
Observation of weakness or collapse
diagnostic_tests: Electrocardiogram (ECG) to detect the absence of atrial contractions
Blood tests (to check for hyperkalemia or other metabolic issues)
Echocardiogram to rule out structural heart disease

other_treatments.purpose: Permanent solution for heart rate control

description: Conduction Blocks occur when the electrical impulses that regulate the heartbeat are partially or fully blocked. This can result in abnormal heart rhythms such as bradycardia and heart block (first-degree, second-degree, or third-degree).
common_species: Dog (especially older dogs or those with underlying heart disease)

physical_examination: Auscultation for bradycardia or pauses
Observation of fainting episodes
diagnostic_tests: Electrocardiogram (ECG) to detect AV blocks
Holter monitor (24-hour ECG) for intermittent blocks
Echocardiogram to assess heart structure

medications.purpose: To increase heart rate during bradycardia episodes

other_treatments.purpose: Permanent solution for third-degree AV block

description: Endocarditis is an infection of the inner lining of the heart, typically affecting the heart valves. It is caused by bacterial infection and can lead to severe complications, including valve damage, heart failure, and systemic infection.
common_species: Dog (especially medium to large breeds), rare in cats

physical_examination: Auscultation of heart murmur
Fever and systemic signs of infection
diagnostic_tests: Blood culture to identify bacteria
Echocardiogram to visualize vegetative growths on valves
Electrocardiogram (ECG) to detect arrhythmias
Blood tests (CBC, biochemistry) to assess infection

other_treatments.purpose: For managing heart failure or shock if present

description: Pericarditis is inflammation of the pericardium, the sac surrounding the heart. It can be caused by infection, trauma, or autoimmune disease, leading to fluid accumulation and reduced heart function.
common_species: Dog (common), cat (rare)

physical_examination: Auscultation of muffled heart sounds
Signs of systemic infection or inflammation
diagnostic_tests: Echocardiogram to visualize pericardial inflammation
Electrocardiogram (ECG) to detect arrhythmias
Chest X-rays to check for fluid accumulation
Blood tests (CBC, biochemistry) to check for systemic inflammation

other_treatments.purpose: Drainage of pericardial fluid if accumulation is significant

description: Myocarditis is inflammation of the heart muscle (myocardium), usually caused by viral, bacterial, or parasitic infections. It can result in heart failure, arrhythmias, and sudden death if severe.
common_species: Dog (especially young dogs), cat (less common)

physical_examination: Auscultation of heart murmurs or irregular beats
Observation of weakness or lethargy
diagnostic_tests: Electrocardiogram (ECG) to detect arrhythmias
Echocardiogram to assess heart muscle function
Blood tests (CBC, biochemistry) to identify infections or inflammation
Cardiac biomarkers (troponin) to assess heart damage

other_treatments.purpose: For managing heart failure and shock

description: Pericardial Effusion is the abnormal accumulation of fluid in the pericardial sac surrounding the heart. It can lead to pressure on the heart, reduced cardiac output, and if untreated, can result in cardiac tamponade.
common_species: Dog (especially large breeds), cat (less common)

physical_examination: Auscultation of muffled heart sounds
Observation of fluid buildup in abdomen
diagnostic_tests: Echocardiogram to detect fluid accumulation around the heart
Chest X-rays to assess fluid buildup and heart size
Electrocardiogram (ECG) to detect electrical changes due to fluid pressure

other_treatments.purpose: Drainage of pericardial fluid to relieve pressure on the heart

description: Cardiac Tamponade is a life-threatening condition caused by the rapid accumulation of fluid in the pericardial sac, which compresses the heart and impairs its ability to pump blood, leading to circulatory collapse.
common_species: Dog (especially large breeds), cat (rare)

physical_examination: Auscultation of muffled heart sounds
Observation of collapse and shock
diagnostic_tests: Echocardiogram to visualize fluid accumulation and heart compression
Chest X-rays to assess heart size and fluid buildup
Blood pressure monitoring to detect hypotension

medications.purpose: To maintain blood pressure during treatment

other_treatments.purpose: Immediate drainage of pericardial fluid to relieve heart compression

description: Pulmonary Hypertension is a condition characterized by abnormally high blood pressure in the arteries of the lungs, leading to strain on the right side of the heart. It can result from heart disease, chronic lung disease, or pulmonary thromboembolism.
common_species: Dog (especially small breeds like Miniature Schnauzers, Dachshunds), rare in cats

physical_examination: Auscultation of heart and lungs for abnormal sounds
Observation of exercise intolerance or collapse
diagnostic_tests: Echocardiogram to visualize heart and assess pulmonary pressure
Chest X-rays to check for signs of heart and lung abnormalities
Blood tests (CBC, biochemistry) to check for underlying causes like heart disease
Electrocardiogram (ECG) to detect right-sided heart enlargement

medications.purpose: To reduce fluid accumulation in lungs

other_treatments.purpose: To assist with breathing in severe cases
To prevent worsening of symptoms

description: Pulmonary Thromboembolism is the sudden blockage of a pulmonary artery by a blood clot, preventing normal blood flow to the lungs. It is often a complication of other conditions, such as heart disease, hypercoagulability, or prolonged immobility.
common_species: Dog (medium to large breeds, especially those with underlying heart disease), rare in cats

physical_examination: Auscultation of lungs for abnormal sounds
Observation of cyanosis and collapse
diagnostic_tests: Chest X-rays to check for signs of pulmonary congestion
Echocardiogram to assess heart function and look for underlying heart disease
Blood gas analysis to detect low oxygen levels
CT scan or pulmonary angiography to confirm the presence of a thrombus

other_treatments.purpose: To improve oxygenation in severe cases
To manage respiratory distress and prevent further complications

description: Heartworm Disease, caused by the parasite Dirofilaria immitis, is transmitted by mosquitoes. The adult worms reside in the pulmonary arteries and right side of the heart, leading to severe heart and lung disease if untreated.
common_species: Dog (especially in areas with high mosquito populations), less common in cats

physical_examination: Auscultation of heart and lungs for abnormal sounds
Observation of coughing and exercise intolerance
diagnostic_tests: Heartworm antigen test to detect adult heartworm presence
Chest X-rays to assess heart size and pulmonary changes
Echocardiogram to visualize heartworm burden in the pulmonary arteries
Blood tests (CBC, biochemistry) to check for secondary effects like anemia or liver damage

other_treatments.purpose: To minimize complications during treatment
For managing heart and lung complications in severe cases

description: Hyperthyroidism-induced cardiomyopathy is a condition in which prolonged hyperthyroidism leads to increased heart rate and metabolic demand, resulting in cardiac enlargement, hypertrophy, and heart failure if untreated.
common_species: Cat (particularly older cats)

physical_examination: Palpation of enlarged thyroid gland, auscultation of heart murmur
diagnostic_tests: Total T4 blood test to confirm hyperthyroidism
Echocardiogram to assess cardiac hypertrophy
Chest X-rays to assess heart size
Electrocardiogram (ECG) to check for arrhythmias

other_treatments.purpose: To destroy hyperactive thyroid tissue

disease_name: Systemic Hypertension (often secondary to kidney disease, hyperadrenocorticism, etc.)
description: Systemic hypertension is abnormally high blood pressure, often secondary to other diseases like kidney disease, hyperadrenocorticism (Cushing’s Disease), or hyperthyroidism. It can lead to complications in the heart, eyes, brain, and kidneys.
common_species: Dog, Cat (common in older animals)

physical_examination: Blood pressure measurement with a Doppler or oscillometric monitor
diagnostic_tests: Blood tests to assess kidney function
Urinalysis to detect proteinuria
Ophthalmic exam to check for retinal detachment
Chest X-rays to assess heart and lung involvement

other_treatments.purpose: Managing primary conditions like kidney disease or Cushing's

description: Anemia-related cardiac stress occurs when reduced red blood cell levels lead to increased workload on the heart, causing tachycardia, weakness, and eventual heart failure in severe cases.
common_species: Dog, Cat

physical_examination: Observation of pale gums and increased heart rate
diagnostic_tests: Complete Blood Count (CBC) to assess red blood cell levels
Chest X-rays to assess heart size and lung involvement
Echocardiogram to assess heart function under stress
Electrocardiogram (ECG) to check for arrhythmias

medications.purpose: For severe anemia to immediately restore red blood cell levels

other_treatments.purpose: Addressing the root cause of anemia, such as kidney disease or blood loss

disease_name: Chronic Kidney Disease with Cardiac Implications
description: Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD) affects the kidneys' ability to filter waste from the blood, leading to systemic hypertension, fluid buildup, and subsequent cardiac stress. CKD often progresses gradually but can lead to heart disease over time.
common_species: Dog, Cat (common in older pets)

physical_examination: Palpation of kidneys, auscultation of heart murmur
diagnostic_tests: Blood tests (BUN, creatinine) to assess kidney function
Urinalysis to detect proteinuria
Blood pressure measurement to detect hypertension
Echocardiogram to assess cardiac involvement

medications.purpose: To reduce blood pressure and protect the kidneys

other_treatments.purpose: Specialized diet to manage kidney disease and reduce cardiac stress
For managing dehydration and maintaining kidney function

description: Cushing's Disease is caused by excessive production of cortisol, often due to a pituitary or adrenal tumor. It leads to systemic complications, including high blood pressure, increased risk of blood clots, and cardiac stress.
common_species: Dog (especially middle-aged to older dogs), rare in cats

physical_examination: Observation of abdominal distension, palpation of liver enlargement
diagnostic_tests: ACTH stimulation test to confirm diagnosis
Low-dose dexamethasone suppression test
Blood pressure measurement to detect hypertension
Chest X-rays to assess heart and lung involvement

other_treatments.purpose: For cases caused by an adrenal tumor

description: Diabetes Mellitus occurs when the body cannot regulate blood sugar, leading to high glucose levels. Over time, this can cause cardiac complications such as systemic hypertension, arrhythmias, and increased risk of heart disease.
common_species: Dog (especially middle-aged to older dogs), Cat

physical_examination: Observation of weight loss, increased thirst, and urination
diagnostic_tests: Blood glucose measurement
Urinalysis to detect glucose or ketones
Fructosamine test to assess long-term blood sugar control
Echocardiogram to assess heart involvement

other_treatments.purpose: Specialized diabetic diet to stabilize blood sugar levels

disease_name: Hypothyroidism (dogs, leading to bradycardia and cardiac enlargement)
description: Hypothyroidism in dogs is a condition where the thyroid gland does not produce enough thyroid hormone, leading to a slow metabolism, weight gain, bradycardia, and cardiac enlargement if untreated.
common_species: Dog (especially middle-aged dogs), rare in cats

physical_examination: Palpation of thyroid gland (usually not enlarged in hypothyroidism), auscultation of heart
diagnostic_tests: Total T4 blood test to confirm hypothyroidism
Echocardiogram to assess cardiac enlargement
Electrocardiogram (ECG) to check for bradycardia
Chest X-rays to assess heart size and lung involvement

other_treatments.purpose: To manage weight gain and metabolic effects of hypothyroidism

description: Hypokalemia is a condition where there is an abnormally low level of potassium in the blood. This can affect nerve and muscle function, including the muscles of the heart, leading to weakness, lethargy, and in severe cases, life-threatening arrhythmias.
common_species: Dog, Cat (especially in chronic kidney disease or excessive fluid loss)

physical_examination: Observation of muscle weakness and lethargy
diagnostic_tests: Blood tests to measure potassium levels
Electrocardiogram (ECG) to detect arrhythmias
Urinalysis to assess kidney function
Blood chemistry panel to check for underlying conditions like kidney disease

medications.purpose: For severe cases requiring immediate correction

other_treatments.purpose: Addressing conditions like kidney disease or fluid loss

description: Hyperkalemia is a condition where there is an abnormally high level of potassium in the blood. It can cause serious heart problems, including life-threatening arrhythmias and cardiac arrest, as well as muscle weakness.
common_species: Dog, Cat (especially in cases of kidney failure, Addison's Disease, or urinary tract obstructions)

physical_examination: Observation of muscle weakness and arrhythmias
diagnostic_tests: Blood tests to measure potassium levels
Electrocardiogram (ECG) to detect arrhythmias
Urinalysis to assess kidney function
Blood chemistry panel to check for kidney disease or Addison's Disease

medications.purpose: To protect the heart from arrhythmias

medications.dosage_dog: 0.25–0.5 U/kg of insulin and 0.5–1 g/kg of dextrose intravenously
medications.purpose: To drive potassium into cells and lower blood levels

other_treatments.purpose: To dilute potassium and restore kidney function

description: Hypocalcemia is an abnormally low level of calcium in the blood. It can affect nerve and muscle function, causing muscle tremors, seizures, and in severe cases, life-threatening cardiac issues.
common_species: Dog, Cat (often secondary to parathyroid disorders, pancreatitis, or eclampsia in lactating animals)

physical_examination: Observation of muscle tremors and restlessness
diagnostic_tests: Blood tests to measure calcium levels
Electrocardiogram (ECG) to detect arrhythmias
Blood chemistry panel to assess kidney function and parathyroid hormone levels
X-rays to rule out bone disorders

medications.purpose: For long-term management of calcium levels

other_treatments.purpose: To assist in calcium absorption

description: Hypercalcemia is an abnormally high level of calcium in the blood, which can lead to a variety of issues including kidney damage, heart arrhythmias, and weakness. It is often associated with underlying diseases like cancer or hyperparathyroidism.
common_species: Dog, Cat (especially with neoplasia, kidney disease, or hyperparathyroidism)

physical_examination: Observation of increased thirst, urination, and lethargy
diagnostic_tests: Blood tests to measure calcium levels
Blood chemistry panel to assess kidney function and parathyroid hormone levels
Chest X-rays to check for neoplasia
Electrocardiogram (ECG) to detect arrhythmias

medications.purpose: To promote calcium excretion through the kidneys
To inhibit bone resorption of calcium

other_treatments.purpose: To dilute calcium and promote kidney function
Addressing causes like cancer or hyperparathyroidism

description: Sepsis-induced cardiac dysfunction occurs when severe systemic infection (sepsis) leads to inflammation and impaired heart function. The inflammatory response can weaken the heart muscle, cause arrhythmias, and lead to heart failure in severe cases.
common_species: Dog, Cat (especially with severe infections or prolonged sepsis)

physical_examination: Auscultation for abnormal heart sounds, observation of low blood pressure and collapse
diagnostic_tests: Blood cultures to identify underlying infections
Echocardiogram to assess heart function
Blood pressure monitoring to detect hypotension
Electrocardiogram (ECG) to detect arrhythmias

other_treatments.purpose: To manage hypotension
To support breathing and improve oxygenation

disease_name: Chronic Lung Diseases Leading to Cor Pulmonale
description: Chronic lung diseases such as chronic bronchitis or emphysema can lead to cor pulmonale, a condition in which right-sided heart failure develops due to increased pressure in the pulmonary arteries. The heart struggles to pump blood through the diseased lungs, causing cardiac stress and failure over time.
common_species: Dog, Cat (particularly older animals with chronic lung conditions)

physical_examination: Auscultation for lung and heart sounds, observation of jugular vein distension
diagnostic_tests: Chest X-rays to assess lung and heart size
Echocardiogram to assess right-sided heart enlargement
Electrocardiogram (ECG) to detect right-sided heart strain
Blood gas analysis to assess oxygen levels

other_treatments.purpose: To improve breathing and oxygenation
To minimize cardiac stress

description: Systemic infections, particularly bacterial infections, can affect the heart by leading to conditions like bacterial endocarditis. In this condition, bacteria colonize the heart valves, leading to valve damage, heart failure, and potential emboli formation.
common_species: Dog, Cat (especially with chronic or untreated bacterial infections)

physical_examination: Auscultation for heart murmurs, observation of fever and systemic signs
diagnostic_tests: Blood cultures to identify bacterial infection
Echocardiogram to detect valve abnormalities or vegetative growths
Chest X-rays to assess heart size and lung involvement
Electrocardiogram (ECG) to detect arrhythmias

medications.purpose: To reduce inflammation and prevent further valve damage

other_treatments.purpose: For cases of severe valve damage
To manage dehydration and systemic infection

description: Aortic thromboembolism (ATE), commonly known as saddle thrombus, occurs when a blood clot forms in the aorta and lodges at the bifurcation of the iliac arteries, leading to paralysis of the hind limbs. This is often a complication of heart disease in cats.
common_species: Cat (especially with heart disease like hypertrophic cardiomyopathy)

physical_examination: Palpation of cold, painful limbs, absence of femoral pulse
diagnostic_tests: Doppler ultrasound to confirm lack of blood flow in the hind limbs
Echocardiogram to assess underlying heart disease
Blood chemistry panel to assess kidney and heart function
Radiographs to assess heart and lung involvement

other_treatments.purpose: Management of paralysis and pain

description: Systemic arterial hypertension is characterized by abnormally high blood pressure in the arteries, often secondary to kidney disease, hyperthyroidism, or hyperadrenocorticism. It can lead to damage in organs like the eyes, heart, brain, and kidneys.
common_species: Dog, Cat (especially older animals or those with kidney disease)

physical_examination: Blood pressure measurement with a Doppler or oscillometric monitor
diagnostic_tests: Blood tests to assess kidney function
Urinalysis to detect proteinuria
Ophthalmic exam to check for retinal detachment
Chest X-rays to assess heart and lung involvement

other_treatments.purpose: Managing primary conditions like kidney disease or Cushing's

description: Pulmonary artery stenosis is a congenital defect that leads to the narrowing of the pulmonary artery, obstructing blood flow from the right ventricle to the lungs. This causes right-sided heart enlargement and can lead to heart failure.
common_species: Dog (especially small breeds like Beagles, English Bulldogs), rare in cats

physical_examination: Auscultation of heart murmur, observation of cyanosis
diagnostic_tests: Echocardiogram to assess the severity of the stenosis
Chest X-rays to assess heart and lung size
Electrocardiogram (ECG) to detect right-sided heart enlargement
Blood tests to assess oxygen levels and kidney function

medications.purpose: To reduce heart rate and improve heart function

other_treatments.purpose: Surgical correction for severe stenosis

description: An aortic aneurysm is a localized bulging or dilation of the aorta due to weakening of the vessel wall. If left untreated, it can lead to rupture, causing severe internal bleeding and sudden death.
common_species: Dog, Cat (rare, usually secondary to trauma or atherosclerosis)
symptoms: Pain in the chest or abdomen

physical_examination: Observation of lethargy, pain, and collapse
diagnostic_tests: Ultrasound or CT scan to visualize the aneurysm
Chest X-rays to assess aortic enlargement
Echocardiogram to assess heart function
Blood pressure monitoring to detect hypertension

medications.purpose: To reduce blood pressure and prevent aneurysm growth

other_treatments.purpose: For cases of large or symptomatic aneurysms

description: Aortic dissection occurs when the inner layer of the aorta tears, causing blood to flow between the layers of the vessel wall. This can result in severe pain, internal bleeding, and sudden death if the aorta ruptures.
common_species: Dog, Cat (rare, often secondary to trauma or hypertension)
symptoms: Sudden onset of severe pain (chest or abdomen)

physical_examination: Observation of sudden collapse, weakness, and pain
diagnostic_tests: Ultrasound or CT scan to visualize the dissection
Chest X-rays to assess aortic enlargement
Blood pressure monitoring to detect hypertension
Blood chemistry to assess kidney and heart function

medications.purpose: To reduce blood pressure and prevent worsening of the dissection

other_treatments.purpose: For cases of large or symptomatic dissections

description: Peripheral vascular disease (PVD) refers to the obstruction of large arteries outside of the heart, often leading to reduced blood flow to the limbs. It can cause pain, lameness, and, in severe cases, tissue death.
common_species: Dog, Cat (rare, often due to thromboembolism or vasculitis)

physical_examination: Palpation of cold, painful limbs, reduced pulse in the affected limb
diagnostic_tests: Doppler ultrasound to assess blood flow in the limbs
Blood tests to assess kidney and heart function
Radiographs to assess bone and tissue damage
Angiography to assess blood vessel obstruction

other_treatments.purpose: To restore blood flow to the affected limb

description: Vasculitis is the inflammation of blood vessels, which can lead to damage to blood vessel walls, restricted blood flow, and ischemia. It can be caused by infections, autoimmune diseases, or drug reactions.
common_species: Dog, Cat

physical_examination: Observation of skin lesions, lameness, and cold extremities
diagnostic_tests: Biopsy of skin lesions to confirm vasculitis
Blood tests to check for autoimmune markers
Angiography to assess blood vessel damage
Urinalysis to check for kidney involvement

other_treatments.purpose: Address bacterial or other infectious causes

description: Hemangiosarcoma is a malignant tumor that originates in the blood vessels, often affecting the heart and causing bleeding, arrhythmias, and heart failure. It is an aggressive cancer that frequently leads to sudden death.
common_species: Dog (especially large breeds like Golden Retrievers, German Shepherds), rare in cats

physical_examination: Observation of weakness, collapse, and irregular heartbeats
diagnostic_tests: Echocardiogram to visualize heart masses or fluid buildup
Chest X-rays to assess heart size and detect tumors
Blood tests to check for anemia and abnormal clotting
CT scan to assess the spread of the tumor

other_treatments.purpose: For localized tumors or when the heart is affected
Management of heart failure and arrhythmias

description: Mitral Valve Prolapse (MVP) occurs when the mitral valve between the left atrium and left ventricle doesn't close properly, causing blood to leak backward into the atrium. This can lead to heart murmurs and, over time, congestive heart failure if left untreated.
common_species: Dog (especially small breeds like Cavalier King Charles Spaniels)

physical_examination: Auscultation of heart murmur, observation of coughing and exercise intolerance
diagnostic_tests: Echocardiogram to assess mitral valve function
Chest X-rays to check for heart enlargement
Electrocardiogram (ECG) to detect arrhythmias
Blood tests to assess kidney function and electrolytes

medications.purpose: To reduce heart workload and manage blood pressure
To reduce fluid buildup in the lungs

other_treatments.purpose: In severe cases where medical management fails

description: Right Ventricular Cardiomyopathy, also known as Boxer Cardiomyopathy, is a genetic condition where the right ventricular myocardium is replaced by fatty or fibrous tissue. This leads to arrhythmias, fainting, and sudden death.
common_species: Dog (especially Boxers)

physical_examination: Auscultation for arrhythmias, observation of fainting or sudden collapse
diagnostic_tests: Electrocardiogram (ECG) to detect arrhythmias
Holter monitor (24-hour ECG) to detect intermittent arrhythmias
Echocardiogram to assess heart function and right ventricular enlargement
Genetic testing for Boxers

medications.purpose: To reduce heart rate and improve heart function

other_treatments.purpose: For severe cases with bradyarrhythmias

description: Patent Foramen Ovale (PFO) is a congenital heart defect where the foramen ovale, a hole in the atrial septum, fails to close after birth. This can result in a heart murmur and inefficiency in blood circulation between the atria.
common_species: Dog (rare in cats)

physical_examination: Auscultation for heart murmur, observation of cyanosis and exercise intolerance
diagnostic_tests: Echocardiogram to visualize the foramen ovale and assess blood flow between the atria
Chest X-rays to assess heart size and pulmonary involvement
Electrocardiogram (ECG) to check for right-sided heart strain
Oxygen saturation test to assess the degree of cyanosis

medications.purpose: To reduce heart rate and improve blood flow

other_treatments.type: Surgical closure of the foramen ovale
other_treatments.purpose: For severe or symptomatic cases

description: Endomyocarditis is the inflammation of both the inner lining (endocardium) and the myocardium of the heart, often caused by bacterial or viral infections. This can lead to heart murmurs, arrhythmias, and eventually heart failure if untreated.
common_species: Dog, Cat (secondary to systemic infections or immune-mediated diseases)

physical_examination: Auscultation for heart murmur, observation of fever and arrhythmias
diagnostic_tests: Blood cultures to identify the underlying infection
Echocardiogram to visualize heart inflammation and valve involvement
Electrocardiogram (ECG) to detect arrhythmias
Chest X-rays to assess heart size

medications.purpose: To reduce inflammation in immune-mediated cases

other_treatments.purpose: For managing heart failure and arrhythmias

description: Myxomatous degeneration refers to the degeneration of heart valves, especially the mitral valve, causing the valve to thicken and become less effective. This leads to valve regurgitation and, eventually, congestive heart failure.
common_species: Dog (especially older small breeds like Poodles and Cavalier King Charles Spaniels)

physical_examination: Auscultation for heart murmur, observation of coughing and exercise intolerance
diagnostic_tests: Echocardiogram to assess valve function and regurgitation
Chest X-rays to check for heart enlargement
Electrocardiogram (ECG) to detect arrhythmias
Blood tests to assess kidney function and electrolytes

medications.purpose: To reduce heart workload and manage blood pressure
To reduce fluid buildup in the lungs

other_treatments.purpose: In severe cases where medical management fails

description: Subaortic Stenosis (SAS) is a congenital defect that causes narrowing below the aortic valve, obstructing blood flow from the left ventricle to the aorta. This leads to left ventricular hypertrophy, heart murmurs, and sudden death in severe cases.
common_species: Dog (large breeds such as Golden Retrievers, Newfoundlands), rare in cats

physical_examination: Auscultation for heart murmurs, observation of exercise intolerance and cyanosis
diagnostic_tests: Echocardiogram to assess the narrowing and left ventricular hypertrophy
Chest X-rays to check for heart enlargement
Electrocardiogram (ECG) to detect arrhythmias
Blood tests to assess kidney and liver function

medications.purpose: To reduce heart rate and prevent arrhythmias

other_treatments.purpose: Surgical correction for severe stenosis

description: Pericardial effusion is the abnormal accumulation of fluid in the pericardial sac surrounding the heart, which compresses the heart and impairs its ability to pump blood effectively. This can lead to heart failure and pericardial tamponade.
common_species: Dog (especially large breeds), rare in cats

physical_examination: Auscultation for muffled heart sounds, observation of jugular vein distension and ascites
diagnostic_tests: Echocardiogram to assess fluid accumulation in the pericardial sac
Chest X-rays to check for heart enlargement and fluid buildup
Electrocardiogram (ECG) to detect electrical changes
Abdominal ultrasound to assess ascites

medications.purpose: To reduce fluid buildup in the lungs and abdomen

other_treatments.purpose: Drainage of pericardial fluid to relieve pressure on the heart

description: Pulmonary Valve Dysplasia is a congenital abnormality where the pulmonary valve does not develop properly, leading to obstructed blood flow from the right ventricle to the lungs. This can result in right-sided heart failure.
common_species: Dog (especially small and large breeds), rare in cats

physical_examination: Auscultation for heart murmurs, observation of cyanosis and exercise intolerance
diagnostic_tests: Echocardiogram to assess the severity of valve dysplasia
Chest X-rays to assess heart and lung size
Electrocardiogram (ECG) to detect right-sided heart strain
Blood gas analysis to assess oxygen levels

medications.purpose: To reduce heart rate and improve heart function

other_treatments.purpose: In severe cases to correct the malformation

description: Eisenmenger's Syndrome is a condition that develops from long-standing left-to-right shunts (due to congenital defects such as ventricular septal defect or atrial septal defect), eventually reversing to a right-to-left shunt. It causes cyanosis, exercise intolerance, and right-sided heart failure.
common_species: Dog, Cat (with long-standing congenital heart defects)

physical_examination: Observation of cyanosis, heart murmur, and exercise intolerance
diagnostic_tests: Echocardiogram to assess the shunt and heart structure
Chest X-rays to assess heart and lung size
Electrocardiogram (ECG) to detect right ventricular hypertrophy
Blood gas analysis to assess oxygen levels

medications.purpose: To reduce heart rate and improve blood flow

other_treatments.type: Surgical correction of underlying congenital defects
other_treatments.purpose: In cases where surgery is possible to reverse the shunt

description: Heartworm Disease, caused by the parasite Dirofilaria immitis, can lead to long-term complications such as pulmonary hypertension and chronic heart failure due to damage caused by the adult heartworms residing in the pulmonary arteries.
common_species: Dog (common in heartworm-endemic areas), rare in cats

physical_examination: Auscultation for heart and lung sounds, observation of abdominal distension and coughing
diagnostic_tests: Heartworm antigen test to detect adult heartworms
Chest X-rays to assess heart and lung size
Echocardiogram to visualize heartworms in the pulmonary arteries
Blood chemistry panel to assess liver and kidney function

medications.purpose: To reduce inflammation in the lungs

other_treatments.purpose: To prevent worsening of heartworm-related damage

description: Pulmonary embolism occurs when a blood clot lodges in the pulmonary arteries, blocking blood flow to the lungs and causing respiratory distress, hypoxia, and heart strain.
common_species: Dog, Cat (secondary to conditions like Cushing's Disease, cancer, or heart failure)

physical_examination: Observation of cyanosis, rapid breathing, and fainting
diagnostic_tests: Chest X-rays to assess heart and lung size
Echocardiogram to assess pulmonary artery involvement
Blood gas analysis to assess oxygen and carbon dioxide levels
CT scan or angiography to confirm the presence of clots

medications.purpose: To improve oxygenation and reduce hypoxia

other_treatments.purpose: For managing heart and lung complications

description: Chemodectomas are slow-growing, usually benign tumors that arise from the chemoreceptor cells located at the base of the heart. These tumors can compress surrounding structures, leading to pericardial effusion and heart failure.
common_species: Dog (especially Brachycephalic breeds like Boxers, Boston Terriers), rare in cats

physical_examination: Observation of jugular vein distension, ascites, and heart sounds
diagnostic_tests: Echocardiogram to assess heart base tumors and fluid accumulation
Chest X-rays to detect masses and pericardial effusion
Electrocardiogram (ECG) to detect arrhythmias
CT or MRI to localize the tumor

other_treatments.purpose: To drain fluid from the pericardial sac
For localized and accessible tumors

description: Lymphoma is a cancer of the lymphocytes that can spread to the heart, particularly in advanced stages of the disease. Cardiac involvement can cause arrhythmias, heart failure, and pericardial effusion.
common_species: Dog, Cat

physical_examination: Observation of heart sounds, jugular vein distension, and weight loss
diagnostic_tests: Echocardiogram to visualize masses or effusion in the heart
Chest X-rays to assess heart size and fluid buildup
Fine needle aspiration (FNA) or biopsy to confirm lymphoma
CT scan to detect cardiac involvement

medications.purpose: To treat lymphoma and reduce cardiac involvement

other_treatments.purpose: To relieve pericardial effusion
For management of heart failure symptoms

description: Endocardial Fibroelastosis is a congenital condition where the inner lining of the heart thickens due to excessive deposition of fibrous and elastic tissue, impairing the heart's ability to pump blood efficiently. This can lead to heart failure.
common_species: Rare in dogs and cats, but documented in some cases.

physical_examination: Auscultation of heart murmur, observation of heart failure symptoms
diagnostic_tests: Echocardiogram to visualize heart thickening and function
Chest X-rays to assess heart size
Electrocardiogram (ECG) to detect arrhythmias
Blood chemistry panel to assess liver and kidney function

other_treatments.purpose: For management of heart failure symptoms

description: Cardiac Amyloidosis occurs when amyloid proteins are deposited in the heart tissue, causing the heart to stiffen. This leads to restrictive cardiomyopathy, making it difficult for the heart to fill with blood.
common_species: Cats (particularly those with systemic amyloidosis), rare in dogs

physical_examination: Observation of heart failure symptoms and arrhythmias
diagnostic_tests: Echocardiogram to assess heart stiffness and function
Biopsy to confirm amyloid deposition in the heart
Blood tests to check kidney and liver function
Electrocardiogram (ECG) to detect arrhythmias

other_treatments.purpose: For managing heart failure symptoms

description: This condition involves arrhythmias occurring in the absence of structural heart disease. It can be caused by systemic illness, electrolyte imbalances, toxins, or idiopathic factors. Examples include supraventricular tachycardia and atrial fibrillation.
common_species: Dog, Cat

physical_examination: Auscultation of irregular heartbeats, observation of fainting and lethargy
diagnostic_tests: Electrocardiogram (ECG) to detect arrhythmias
Holter monitor to record 24-hour ECG activity
Blood tests to check for electrolyte imbalances
Echocardiogram to rule out structural heart disease

other_treatments.purpose: In cases of severe bradyarrhythmias

description: Arteriovenous fistulas are abnormal connections between arteries and veins that bypass the capillary system, causing abnormal blood flow. This can overload the heart, leading to heart failure over time.
common_species: Dog, rare in cats

physical_examination: Auscultation of heart murmur, observation of jugular vein distension and exercise intolerance
diagnostic_tests: Echocardiogram to assess abnormal blood flow
Doppler ultrasound to visualize blood flow in arteries and veins
Chest X-rays to assess heart size and shape
CT scan to confirm the presence of fistulas

medications.purpose: To reduce heart rate and improve blood flow

other_treatments.purpose: For correcting abnormal connections between arteries and veins

description: CTEPH is a rare form of pulmonary hypertension caused by unresolved blood clots in the pulmonary arteries. Over time, these blockages lead to increased pressure in the pulmonary arteries, right-sided heart failure, and respiratory distress.
common_species: Dogs, especially those with a history of pulmonary embolism

physical_examination: Observation of labored breathing, coughing, and fainting
diagnostic_tests: Chest X-rays to assess lung and heart size
Echocardiogram to evaluate right-sided heart strain
Blood gas analysis to assess oxygen levels
Pulmonary angiography to detect clots

other_treatments.purpose: To improve breathing and oxygenation
